entries.meaning: The ocean of compassion smiled and told the ferryman to do whatever would keep his boat from being lost: bring water quickly, wash my feet, and take us across without delay. People cross the immeasurable ocean of becoming by remembering Rāma's name just once, yet that same compassionate lord entreated the ferryman—the one for whom the three-stepped universe was too small. The divine river rejoiced to behold his toenails, while Sītā, hearing his words, drew his mind's meaning toward her own. Having received Rāma's command, the boatman brought a wooden basin filled with water. Brimming with the highest joy and love, he began to wash the lotus feet. All the gods rained flowers and acclaimed him, saying no store of merit equaled his. The ferryman drank the foot-water with his family, carried his ancestors across, and then joyfully ferried the lord to the other bank.

Rāma, Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, and Guha stepped ashore upon the sand of the Gaṅgā. The ferryman disembarked and prostrated. Rāma felt embarrassed that he had nothing to give him. Sītā, who understood her beloved's heart, gladly removed a jeweled ring. The compassionate lord offered it as the fare, but the ferryman seized his feet in distress: Lord, what have I not gained today? The fires of fault, sorrow, poverty, and suffering are extinguished. I have worked for a very long time, but today Fate has given me abundant and excellent wages. I desire nothing more, lord; your grace, compassionate friend of the lowly, is enough. On the return crossing, give me whatever you will; I shall receive that gift upon my head. Though Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā pressed him repeatedly, the boatman took nothing. The abode of compassion dismissed him only after granting the boon of stainless devotion.

Raghunātha then bathed, worshiped a clay emblem of Śiva, and bowed his head. Sītā joined her hands and prayed to the celestial river: Mother, fulfill my wish, so that I may safely return with my husband and brother-in-law and worship you as befits you. Hearing Sītā's plea steeped in the nectar of love, the pure water gave voice to an excellent blessing: Vaidehī, beloved of Raghu's hero, hear me. The world knows your power; the guardians of the worlds arise at your glance, and all their perfections stand with joined hands to serve you. That you have offered so great a plea to me is your compassion, for by it you have bestowed greatness upon me. Even so, goddess, I shall bless you, so that my speech may prove fruitful: with the lord of your life and his brother you will return safely to Kosala, fulfill every heart's desire in worship, and your noble fame will cover the world.

Sītā rejoiced to hear the auspicious words of the Gaṅgā, now favorable to her. Rāma then told Guha to go home. At once Guha's face withered and his heart burned. Joining his hands, he humbly asked the jewel of Raghu's line to hear his plea: let me remain with you four days, serve your feet, and show you the road. When we reach the forest where you will dwell, I shall make you a beautiful leaf-hut; afterward, lord, give whatever command you wish, and by Rāma's name I shall obey. Rāma recognized his natural affection and took Guha along, filling his heart with delight. Guha next called his kinsmen, satisfied them, and sent them home. Remembering Gaṇeśa and Śiva and bowing to the celestial river, Raghunātha set out for the forest with Sītā, his younger brother, and his friend.

That day they lodged beneath a tree, and Lakṣmaṇa and the friend arranged every comfort. At dawn Rāma performed the morning rites and saw Prayāga, sovereign of holy places. In the poet's royal allegory, Truth was its minister, Faith its beloved queen, and Mādhava its peerless helpful friend. The four aims of life filled its treasury, and the blessed region formed a most lovely realm. Its inaccessible territory and strong, handsome fort could not be reached by an enemy even in a dream. Its entire army consisted of the finest heroic pilgrimages, valiant destroyers of the battalions of sin. The confluence shone as its throne; the imperishable banyan was a parasol enchanting the sages' minds; the waves of Yamunā and Gaṅgā were fly-whisks whose sight broke sorrow and poverty. Pure saints of good deeds served there and obtained every heart's desire, while companies of Vedas and Purāṇas sang the stainless multitude of its virtues as bards.

Who can describe Prayāga's power? It is a lion against the elephant herd of accumulated sins. Seeing such a beautiful lord of holy places, Raghu's hero, an ocean of happiness, felt joy. He praised the sovereign pilgrimage with his own lips, speaking to Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, and his friend. They bowed and, while viewing forest and garden, lovingly recounted its greatness. In this way they came to the confluence, whose remembrance grants every auspicious blessing. They joyfully bathed, worshiped Śiva, and honored the deities of the pilgrimage according to rule. Then the lord came to Bharadvāja; as Rāma prostrated, the sage clasped him to his heart. The sage's delight cannot be told: it was as though he had gained the very mass of brahmic bliss. The great seer blessed him, inwardly overjoyed, regarding the fruit of his merit as brought by Fate directly within his eyes' reach.

Bharadvāja asked after their welfare, gave them seats, and completed their welcome with loving worship. He brought fine roots, fruits, tubers, and shoots that seemed to spring from the nectar of his own mind. Rāma gladly ate the roots and fruit with Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, Guha, and the attendants, and all their weariness departed. Then Bharadvāja spoke gently: today my austerity and pilgrimage are fruitful; today my recitation, yoga, and detachment bear fruit. Every auspicious discipline and its equipment are fulfilled today because I behold you, Rāma. There is no second limit of gain or happiness: the hope of seeing you has been completely fulfilled. Now show me this grace and grant this boon—natural love for the lotus of your feet. As long as a person is not yours without deceit in deed, word, and mind, not even millions of remedies bring happiness, even in a dream.

Hearing the sage's words, Rāma felt shy, while Bharadvāja was replete with the joy of loving devotion. Then Rāma praised the sage's lovely renown in millions of ways before everyone: whoever receives your honor, great seer, is truly great and the home of every virtue. Sage and Raghu's hero bowed to one another and experienced a joy beyond the reach of speech. When news spread, residents of Prayāga—students, ascetics, sages, perfected beings, and renunciants—came together to Bharadvāja's hermitage to see Daśaratha's lovely sons. Rāma bowed to everyone; gladdened by the reward granted their eyes, they blessed him and returned while praising his beauty. Rāma rested that night, bathed at Prayāga in the morning, and set out with Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, and Guha, joyfully bowing his head to the sage.

Rāma lovingly asked the sage which road they should take. Bharadvāja smiled inwardly and replied that every road was easy for Rāma. He summoned disciples to accompany them; fifty came gladly, each professing immeasurable love and asking to show the way. The sage sent four students who had earned the merit of many lives. Rāma bowed, received the seer's permission, and set out with a joyful heart. Whenever they passed near a village, men and women ran to see them. Their birth bore fruit and they felt protected, but returned sorrowfully, sending their hearts along. At Rāma's humble request the students took leave after attaining their hearts' desire. The travelers descended to bathe in the Yamunā's water, dark as Rāma's own body.

Hearing of them, the men and women along the riverbank left their individual tasks and hurried out. Seeing Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, and Sītā's beauty, they praised their own great fortune. Though inwardly eager, they were shy to ask the travelers' names and home. The wise elders among them devised a way and recognized Rāma; they told everyone the whole story, that he was going to the forest in obedience to his father's command. Hearing this, all grieved and regretted it, saying king and queen had not acted well. At that moment a young ascetic arrived, handsome, small in years, and a mass of spiritual radiance. His movement was unfathomable even to a poet; he wore the garb of detachment and loved Rāma in thought, deed, and word. With tearful eyes and body thrilling, he recognized his chosen deity and fell flat upon the earth; his condition was beyond description.
